In recent years, researchers have increasingly focused on directly parameterizing dynamic controllers and optimizing the LQG cost over the resulting parameterized set. However, this parameterization typically gives rise to a highly non-convex optimization landscape for the resulting parameterized LQG problem. To our knowledge, there is currently no general method for certifying the global optimality of candidate controller parameters in this setting. In this work, we address these gaps with the following contributions. First, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for the global optimality of stationary points in a parameterized LQG problem. This condition reduces the verification of optimality to a test of the controllability and observability for a novel, specially constructed transfer function, yielding a precise and computationally tractable certificate. Furthermore, our condition provides a rigorous explanation for why traditional parameterizations can lead to suboptimal stationary points. Second, we elevate the controller parameter space from conventional finite-dimensional settings to the infinite-dimensional $\mathcal{RH}_\infty$ space and develop a gradient-based algorithm in this setting, for which we provide a theoretical analysis establishing global convergence. Finally, representative numerical experiments validate the theoretical findings and demonstrate the practical viability of the proposed approach. Additionally, the appendix section explores a data-driven extension to the model-free setting, where we outline a parameter estimation scheme and demonstrate its practical viability through numerical simulation.

papers.title: The invisible hand as an emergent property
papers.abstract: We develop a multi-sector competitive economy where firms reallocate across sectors under myopic profit-seeking behaviour and quadratic reallocation costs. The dynamic path, formalised as a gradient flow in Wasserstein space, yields two emergent properties: (i) short-run equilibria can be seen as solutions to sequential aggregate optimisation problems; and (ii) the long-run equilibrium is globally stable and efficient. Linearizing around the common long-run equilibrium, we show that convergence can be faster or slower under a planner who accounts for reallocation costs than under decentralized adjustment.

papers.title: Effective and Efficient Attributed Hypergraph Embedding on Nodes and Hyperedges
papers.abstract: An attributed hypergraph comprises nodes with attributes and hyperedges that connect varying numbers of nodes. Attributed hypergraph node and hyperedge embedding (AHNEE) maps nodes and hyperedges to compact vectors for use in important tasks such as node classification, hyperedge link prediction, and hyperedge classification. Generating high-quality embeddings is challenging due to the complexity of attributed hypergraphs and the need to embed both nodes and hyperedges, especially in large-scale data. Existing solutions often fall short by focusing only on nodes or lacking native support for attributed hypergraphs, leading to inferior quality, and struggle with scalability on large attributed hypergraphs. We propose SAHE, an efficient and effective approach that unifies node and hyperedge embeddings for AHNEE computation, advancing the state of the art via comprehensive embedding formulations and algorithmic designs. First, we introduce two higher-order similarity measures, HMS-N and HMS-E, to capture similarities between node pairs and hyperedge pairs, respectively. These measures consider multi-hop connections and global topology within an extended hypergraph that incorporates attribute-based hyperedges. SAHE formulates the AHNEE objective to jointly preserve all-pair HMS-N and HMS-N similarities. Direct optimization is computationally expensive, so we analyze and unify core approximations of all-pair HMS-N and HMS-N to solve them simultaneously. To enhance efficiency, we design several non-trivial optimizations that avoid iteratively materializing large dense matrices while maintaining high-quality results. Extensive experiments on diverse attributed hypergraphs and 3 downstream tasks, compared against 11 baselines, show that SAHE consistently outperforms existing methods in embedding quality and is up to orders of magnitude faster.

papers.title: A Bayesian approach to model uncertainty in single-cell genomic data
papers.abstract: Network models provide a powerful framework for analysing single-cell count data, facilitating the characterisation of cellular identities, disease mechanisms, and developmental trajectories. However, uncertainty modeling in unsupervised learning with genomic data remains insufficiently explored. Conventional clustering methods assign a singular identity to each cell, potentially obscuring transitional states during differentiation or mutation. This study introduces a variational Bayesian framework for clustering and analysing single-cell genomic data, employing a Bayesian Gaussian mixture model with Dirichlet priors to estimate the probabilistic association of cells with distinct clusters. This approach captures cellular transitions, yielding biologically coherent insights into neurogenesis and breast cancer progression. The inferred clustering probabilities enable further analyses, including Differential Expression Analysis and pseudotime analysis. We propose the Area Under the Curve as a novel way of quantifying clustering performance in relation to cell-type specific marker genes, as it better captures the clustering characteristics of interest and aligns closely with visual assessments in the scRNA-seq data. To summarise, this methodological advancement enhances the resolution of single-cell data analysis, enabling a more nuanced characterisation of dynamic cellular identities in development and disease.

papers.title: RoboMemory: A Brain-inspired Multi-memory Agentic Framework for Interactive Environmental Learning in Physical Embodied Systems
papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks require agents to learn, reason, and generalize robustly across complex real-world environments. However, existing approaches often struggle with partial observability, fragmented spatial reasoning, and inefficient integration of heterogeneous memories, limiting their capacity for long-horizon adaptation. To address this, we introduce RoboMemory, a brain-inspired framework that unifies Temporal, Spatial, Semantic, and Episodic memory for efficient long-horizon planning and interactive learning. Its core innovations are a comprehensive memory system designed for embodied tasks, and a dynamic spatial knowledge graph for scalable, consistent memory updates. Extensive experiments on EmbodiedBench show that RoboMemory improves the average success rate of Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Ins by 26.5 percentage points and achieves performance comparable to strong closed-source VLM agents. Real-world trials further suggest RoboMemory's potential for interactive environmental learning by reusing accumulated experience across repeated task attempts. These results demonstrate RoboMemory as a scalable memory-augmented framework for embodied agents, improving long-horizon planning and cumulative learning in complex interactive environments.

papers.title: Optimal Calibration of Qubit Detuning and Crosstalk
papers.abstract: Characterizing and calibrating physical qubits is essential for maintaining the performance of quantum processors. A key challenge in this process is the presence of crosstalk that complicates the estimation of individual qubit detunings. In this work, we derive optimal strategies for estimating detuning and crosstalk parameters by optimizing Ramsey interference experiments using Fisher information and the Cramer-Rao bound. We compare several calibration protocols, including measurements of a single quadrature at multiple times and of two quadratures at a single time, for a fixed number of total measurements. Our results predict that the latter approach yields the highest precision and robustness in both cases of isolated and coupled qubits. We validate experimentally our approach using a single NV center as well as superconducting transmons. Our approach enables accurate parameter extraction with significantly fewer measurements, resulting in up to a 50% reduction in calibration time while maintaining estimation accuracy.

papers.title: Advancing AI Capabilities and Evolving Labor Outcomes
papers.abstract: This paper examines how labor market outcomes have evolved across occupations as AI capabilities advanced from generative AI chatbots to reasoning models and AI agents. We construct an occupational AI exposure score that measures the share of each occupation's work that AI could perform at each capability stage, and link the change in exposure to the Current Population Survey from January 2023 through June 2026, using first-difference and fixed-effects designs at the occupation and individual level, with 2017 to 2022 as a placebo period. We find that occupations with larger increases in exposure show no change in employment or unemployment relative to occupations with comparable workforces. However, the composition of the workforce in these occupations changed. The number of workers under 30 decreased by about 8 percent per standard deviation of the change in exposure, and the decline is concentrated among workers without a college degree and builds gradually from 2023. It is not accompanied by higher unemployment among young workers who were already in these occupations, which suggests a decline in entry rather than an increase in exit. The decline is smaller when remote work is held fixed, but it remains. On the other hand, college graduates aged 30 to 49 gained full-time employment. Part-time work declined, weekly hours increased slightly, and the workforce in these occupations became older and more educated. In sum, the early effects of AI appear in the composition of the workforce rather than in the number of jobs.

papers.title: Regularized Extragradient Methods for Solving Equilibrium Problems on Hadamard Manifolds
papers.abstract: Employing two distinct types of regularization terms, we propose two regularized extragradient methods for solving equilibrium problems on Hadamard manifolds. The sequences generated by these extragradient algorithms converge to a solution of the equilibrium problem without requiring the Lipschitz continuity of the bifunction and without an upper bound on the regularization parameters. We establish convergence results for both algorithms under a monotonicity condition. When the bifunction is additionally strongly pseudomonotone, we derive global error bounds and establish $R$-linear convergence rates. Finally, we present numerical experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods.

papers.title: Science Prospects for the Southern Wide-field Gamma-ray Observatory: SWGO
papers.abstract: Ground-based gamma-ray astronomy is now well established as a key observational approach to address critical topics at the frontiers of astroparticle physics and high-energy astrophysics. Whilst the field of TeV astronomy was once dominated by arrays of atmospheric Cherenkov Telescopes, ground-level particle detection has now been demonstrated to be an equally viable and strongly complementary approach. Ground-level particle detection provides continuous monitoring of the overhead sky, critical for the mapping of extended structures and capturing transient phenomena. As demonstrated by HAWC and LHAASO, the technique provides the best available sensitivity above a few tens of TeV, and for the first time access to the PeV energy range. Despite the success of this approach, there is so far no major ground-level particle-based observatory with access to the Southern sky. HESS, located in Namibia, is the only major gamma-ray instrument in the Southern Hemisphere, and has shown the extraordinary richness of the inner galaxy in the TeV band, but is limited in terms of field of view and energy reach. SWGO is an international effort to construct the first wide-field instrument in the south with deep sensitivity from 100s of GeV into the PeV domain. The project is now close to the end of its development phase and planning for construction of the array in Chile has begun. Here we describe the baseline design, expected sensitivity and resolution, and describe in detail the main scientific topics that will be addressed by this new facility and its initial phase SWGO-A. We show that SWGO will have a transformational impact on a wide range of topics from cosmic-ray acceleration and transport to the nature of dark matter. SWGO represents a key piece of infrastructure for multi-messenger astronomy in the next decade, with strong scientific synergies with the nearby CTA Observatory.

papers.title: Highly Efficient and Effective LLMs with Multi-Boolean Architectures
papers.abstract: Weight binarization has emerged as a promising strategy to reduce the complexity of large language models (LLMs). Existing approaches fall into post-training binarization, which is simple but causes severe performance loss, and training-aware methods, which depend on full-precision latent weights, adding complexity and limiting efficiency. We propose a novel framework that represents LLMs with multi-kernel Boolean parameters and, for the first time, enables direct finetuning LMMs in the Boolean domain, eliminating the need for latent weights. This enhances representational capacity and dramatically reduces complexity during both finetuning and inference. Extensive experiments across diverse LLMs show our method outperforms recent ultra low-bit quantization and binarization techniques.

papers.title: Iterative Orthogonalization Scaling Laws
papers.abstract: The muon optimizer has picked up much attention as of late as a possible replacement to the seemingly omnipresent Adam optimizer. Recently, care has been taken to document the scaling laws of hyper-parameters under muon such as weight decay and learning rate. However, at much larger scales the iterative orthogonalization procedure present in muon may suffer a possible issue as the singular values of random matrices shrink with scale. This paper shows this scaling behavior theoretically and empirically on random matrices but does not suggest what to do about it.

papers.title: Identifying Macro Causal Effects in a C-DMG over ADMGs
papers.abstract: Causal effect identification using causal graphs is a fundamental challenge in causal inference. While extensive research has been conducted in this area, most existing methods assume the availability of fully specified directed acyclic graphs or acyclic directed mixed graphs. However, in complex domains such as medicine and epidemiology, complete causal knowledge is often unavailable, and only partial information about the system is accessible. This paper focuses on causal effect identification within partially specified causal graphs, with particular emphasis on cluster-directed mixed graphs (C-DMGs) which can represent many different acyclic directed mixed graphs (ADMGs). These graphs provide a higher-level representation of causal relationships by grouping variables into clusters, offering a more practical approach for handling complex systems. Unlike fully specified ADMGs, C-DMGs can contain cycles, which complicate their analysis and interpretation. Furthermore, their cluster-based nature introduces new challenges, as it gives rise to two distinct types of causal effects: macro causal effects and micro causal effects, each with different properties. In this work, we focus on macro causal effects, which describe the effects of entire clusters on other clusters. We establish that the do-calculus is both sound and complete for identifying these effects in C-DMGs over ADMGs when the cluster sizes are either unknown or of size greater than one. Additionally, we provide a graphical characterization of non-identifiability for macro causal effects in these graphs.

papers.title: Barriers to dequantization of near-term molecular electronic structure methods
papers.abstract: We prove classical simulation hardness, under the generalized $\mathsf{P}\neq\mathsf{NP}$ conjecture, for quantum circuit families with applications in near-term molecular electronic ground and excited state estimation. The proof exploits a connection to particle number conserving matchgate circuits with fermionic magic state inputs, which are shown to be universal for quantum computation under postselection, and are therefore not classically simulable in the worst case, in either the strong (multiplicative) or weak (sampling) sense. We apply these results to non-orthogonal quantum eigensolvers designed for near-term hardware by ruling out sample-based dequantization strategies to additively approximate the off-diagonal matrix elements between orbital-rotated correlated reference states that satisfy an irreducible fermionic magic property, which combines anticoncentration in any orbital basis with an average-case multiplicative approximation hardness conjecture for the associated matrix polynomials. We apply this complexity analysis to two choices of ansatz that incorporate both static and dynamic correlations to model the electronic eigenstates of molecular systems. These are linear combinations of orbital-rotated matrix product states, which are preparable in linear depth, and linear combinations of states prepared by generalized unitary coupled cluster with singles and doubles or unitary cluster Jastrow circuits of polynomial depth, for which computing the expectation values of local fermionic observables up to a constant additive error is $\mathsf{BQP}$-complete. We discuss the implications for achieving practical quantum advantage in resolving the electronic structure of catalytic systems composed from multivalent transition metal atoms using near-term quantum hardware.

papers.title: Reward Shaping to Mitigate Reward Hacking in RLHF
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is widely used to align large language models with human preferences, but it remains vulnerable to \emph{reward hacking}, whereby a policy exploits flaws in the reward function at the expense of the intended behavior. Reward shaping can stabilize training and partially mitigate reward hacking, yet its design principles remain underexplored. Our systematic study of common shaping methods suggests that shaped rewards should be bounded and should rise rapidly before gradually saturating. We introduce \emph{Preference as Reward} (PAR), which applies a sigmoid to centered rewards to produce a signal that reflects the reward model's latent preferences. We show that PAR has a variance-reduction property that stabilizes training and substantially widens the window for effective early stopping. Using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and Gemma2-2B, PAR consistently outperforms the other shaping methods evaluated and demonstrates high data efficiency and robustness. Comparisons with unshaped rewards across four base models and four reinforcement learning algorithms show that PAR is effective across models and particularly beneficial for actor--critic methods when value estimates become unstable. The code is available at https://github.com/PorUna-byte/PAR.

papers.title: Spurious Isospin Breaking in the In-medium Similarity Renormalization Group
papers.abstract: The in-medium similarity renormalization group is a promising ab initio approach for computing the isospin-related theoretical correction $δ_C$ to superallowed beta decay rates, relevant for tests of CKM unitarity. An essential requirement of such corrections is a properly quantified theoretical uncertainty. While isospin symmetry is explicitly broken by internucleon forces, approximations made in the solving the many-body problem can also spuriously break the symmetry, obscuring the desired signal. In this work, we use a toy model to identify the primary sources of spurious isospin symmetry breaking introduced by the IMSRG many-body framework, and provide mitigation strategies for application in large-scale calculations.

papers.title: Class number of real quadratic fields of explicit discriminant
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the class numbers of a family of real quadratic fields $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{D})$ whose discriminants possess a specific exponential structure. More precisely, the discriminant $D$ is given by $(b(4bs+1)^k+s)^2 + (4bs+1)^k$, where $b$, $s$ and $k$ are positive integers, and $D$ is assumed to be square-free. This non-Richaud-Degert family is characterized by a predictable continued fraction expansion for $\sqrt{D}$, which allows for an explicit expression of its fundamental unit. When the parameters $b$ and $s$ are fixed, the corresponding regulators grow asymptotically like $(\log D)^2$. By analyzing the associated partial twisted zeta functions at $z=0$ and applying algebraic methods inspired by the strategies of Biró, we derive explicit criteria under which the class number $h(D)$ is strictly greater than $1$. Our work contributes to the long-standing mathematical tradition that aims to solve the "class number one problem" for explicit families of real quadratic fields.

papers.title: Phase transitions in the simplicial Ising model on hypergraphs
papers.abstract: Complex higher-order interactions can reshape higher-order dynamics in complex systems. Systematic understanding of the repertoire of phase transitions that higher-order interactions can trigger remains incomplete. Here we study the phase transitions in the simplicial Ising model on hypergraphs, in which the energy within each hyperedge is lowered only when all the member spins are unanimously aligned. We show that its Hamiltonian is equivalent to a weighted sum of lower-order interactions and use the Landau free energy to identify diverse phase transitions depending on the hyperedge sizes. For $q$-uniform hypergraphs, the nature of transitions shifts from continuous to discontinuous at the tricritical point $q = 4$. When both pairwise edges and hyperedges of size $q > 2$ coexist, diverse scenarios emerge, including mixed-order and double transitions, for $q > 8$. We further adopt the Bethe--Peierls method to investigate the interplay between pairwise and higher-order interactions in achieving global magnetization, illuminating the multiscale nature of double transitions.

papers.title: Does quantum mechanics apply to macroscopic objects? How to define macro?
papers.abstract: According to Quantum Mechanics a narrow wave-packet of the center of mass of any macroscopic object should smear out after some time. The problem is usually waved out by assuming that due to their heavy masses this occurs over astronomical times. Without a clear definition of macroscopic objects this remains ambiguous. On the other hand, Quantum Mechanics allows and energetically even prefers largely smeared out c.m. states that never been seen. Why is this the real state of the world we know? Does it suggest a micro-macro threshold with different theoretical descriptions? Does offer micro-miniaturization a hope for answering these questions?

papers.title: The Bruce-Roberts Tjurina number of holomorphic 1-forms along complex analytic varieties
papers.abstract: We introduce the notion of the \textit{Bruce-Roberts Tjurina number} for holomorphic 1-forms with respect to a pair $(X,V)$ of complex analytic subvarieties. We characterize its finiteness and, when $X$ and $V$ are hypersurfaces with at most isolated singularities, relate it to a determinantal colength, the Tjurina number of the 1-form with respect to $V$, and the Tjurina number of $X$. We also establish a decomposition of the difference between the Bruce-Roberts Milnor and Tjurina numbers and a bound for their quotient. As an application, we prove a relative quasihomogeneity result for germs of non-dicritical generalized curve foliations in complex dimension two.

papers.title: Large Deviations Principle for Bures-Wasserstein Barycenters
papers.abstract: We prove the large deviations principle for empirical Bures-Wasserstein barycenters of independent, identically-distributed samples of covariance matrices and covariance operators. As an application, we explore some consequences of our results for the phenomenon of dimension-free concentration of measure for Bures-Wasserstein barycenters. Our theory reveals a novel notion of exponential tilting in the Bures-Wasserstein space, which, in analogy with Cramér's theorem in the Euclidean case, solves the relative entropy projection problem under a constraint on the barycenter. Notably, this method of proof is easy to adapt to other geometric settings of interest; with the same method, we obtain large deviations principles for empirical barycenters in Riemannian manifolds and the univariate Wasserstein space, and we obtain large deviations upper bounds for empirical barycenters in the general multivariate Wasserstein space. In fact, our results are the first known large deviations principles for Fréchet means in any non-linear metric space.

papers.title: Scalable and Calibrated Sampling for Bayesian Generalized Linear Mixed Model via Stochastic Gradient Markov Chain Monte Carlo
papers.abstract: Generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) are widely used for analyzing correlated data, particularly in large-scale biomedical and social science applications. Scalable Bayesian inference for GLMMs is challenging due to an intractable marginal likelihood and a high computational cost incurred by conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. We develop a stochastic gradient MCMC (SGMCMC) algorithm tailored to GLMMs that enables accurate posterior inference in the large-sample regime. Our approach uses Fisher's identity to construct a (biased) Monte Carlo estimator of the gradient of the marginal log-likelihood, making SGMCMC feasible when direct gradient computation is impossible. We analyze the additional variability, introduced by both data subsampling and gradient approximation, to derive a post-hoc covariance correction that yields properly calibrated posterior uncertainty. We show through simulated studies that the proposed method provides accurate posterior means and variances in settings with a large number of groups, outperforming existing approaches, including control variate methods. We further demonstrate the method's practical utility in an analysis of electronic health records data, where accounting for variance inflation materially changes scientific conclusions.

papers.title: Local Projections Inference with High-Dimensional Covariates without Exact Sparsity
papers.abstract: This paper develops a high-dimensional local projections framework for estimating impulse responses in the presence of many potential controls. Other approaches often rely on exact sparsity assumptions, but empirical macroeconomic applications may involve nuisance relationships better described by structured coefficient decay. Building on the orthogonal greedy algorithm with high-dimensional AIC (OGA+HDAIC), I propose a double-selection procedure that separately addresses the shock equation and the outcome equation within local projections. The method allows for nonexact sparsity through polynomially decaying nuisance coefficients, with rates indexed by the decay exponent rather than by an effective sparsity level. Under suitable moment, dependence, and approximation conditions, the estimator achieves asymptotic normality with HAC standard errors. Simulation evidence shows reliable coverage under shock contamination and lower point-estimation error under predictable high-dimensional outcome nuisance. I illustrate the method's practical feasibility in a monetary policy application using the FRED-MD dataset.

papers.title: Reverse inequality for the Riesz transforms on Riemannian manifolds
papers.abstract: Let M be a complete Riemannian manifold satisfying the doubling volume condition for geodesic balls and L^q scaled Poincar{é} inequalities on suitable remote balls for some q<2. We prove the inequality $||Δ^{1/2}f||\_p\lesssim ||\nabla f||\_p$ for all p $\in$ (q, 2], which generalizes previous results due to Auscher and Coulhon. Our conclusion applies, in particular, when M has a finite number of Euclidean ends. The proof strongly relies on Hardy inequalities, which are also new in this context and of independent interest.

papers.title: Cavitation near the oscillating piezoelectric plate in water
papers.abstract: Gas and vapor bubbles at a wall can reduce the skin friction of a liquid flow. We estimate whether an oscillating piezoelectric plate mounted flush with the wall can create such a near-wall bubble layer by acoustic cavitation. Once the cavitation threshold is reached, the liquid can no longer follow the receding plate, and the excess plate displacement is accommodated by cavitation bubbles forming at the wall; this kinematic argument gives the bubble volume generated per stroke and its energy cost. Homogeneous cavitation in pure water (about -30 MPa) requires pressure amplitudes far beyond those of flat piezoelectric plates and produces submicron bubbles that collapse within nanoseconds. Heterogeneous cavitation on wall and gas nuclei (-0.1 to -1 MPa) is within reach of piezoceramics and concentrates the void on fewer, larger wal-attached bubbles, which survive between strokes if they exceed a few micrometres at 5 MHz. The acoustic power needed to sustain a bubble layer in a turbulent boundary layer at 10 m/s is about 20 kW/m2 for heterogeneous and about 0.4 MW/m2 for homogeneous cavitation.

papers.title: Bundling Complements
papers.abstract: I study a monopolist selling goods to a buyer with combinatorial preferences. The dual of the seller's problem is a minimum-cost flow of the differential virtual value. I characterize when the type distribution alone determines the differential virtual value. The distribution then determines the *required directions*, along which the dual transports mass, and the preference determines the *covered directions* of each bundle; optimality is full coverage. This separation enables comparative statics in the preference: raising a complementarity premium on bundles containing a core of goods widens their covered directions. Two premium thresholds describe the optimum: above a lower threshold the grand bundle must be offered; above an upper threshold a *core-peripheral* menu --- a bundled core with optional add-ons not sold standalone --- is optimal, and every optimal menu is core-peripheral. The upper threshold is finite if and only if the menu is *inclusive*: it excludes no near-top buyer.

papers.title: Event-Based Control via Sparsity-Promoting Regularization: A Rollout Approach with Performance Guarantees
papers.abstract: This paper presents a controller design framework aiming to balance control performance and actuation rate. Control performance is evaluated by an infinite-horizon average cost, and the number of control actions is penalized via sparsity-promoting regularization. Since the formulated optimal control problem has a combinatorial nature, we employ a rollout algorithm to obtain a tractable suboptimal solution. In the proposed scheme, actuation timings are determined through a multistage minimization procedure based on a receding-horizon approach, and the corresponding control inputs are computed online. We establish theoretical performance guarantees with respect to periodic control and prove the stability of the closed-loop system. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through a numerical example.

papers.title: On the Theoretical Foundations of Data Exchange Economies
papers.abstract: Organizations increasingly seek to share and access datasets to improve their ML models and derive insights. Despite the immense demand for quality data, data exchange and collaboration have not reached their full potential, as cited by the European Commission. One of the key reasons is the lack of reciprocity, where some participants perceive their contribution to others to be of higher value than what they receive in return. We propose a general framework for data exchange without payments, focusing on two main properties: (i) reciprocal fairness, which ensures that each agent receives utility proportional to their contribution to the total welfare -- contributions are quantifiable using well-established credit-sharing functions such as the Shapley share and proportional share, and (ii) core-stability, which guarantees that no coalition of agents can identify an exchange among themselves which they all unanimously prefer to the current exchange. Surprisingly, we show that fair and stable exchanges exist for all monotone continuous utility functions. Building on this, we investigate the computational complexity of finding approximate fair and stable exchanges. We present a local search algorithm for instances with monotone submodular utility functions and cross-monotone credit-sharing functions, e.g., Shapley share. We prove that this problem belongs to CLS ($=$ PPAD $\cap$ PLS) under mild assumptions. Our framework opens up several intriguing theoretical avenues for future research on data economics.

papers.title: Beyond the Mean Gap: What Transferred-Angle QAOA Retains on a Superconducting Processor
papers.abstract: Hardware executions of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) are often validated by comparing the device's mean cost with a simulation, a check that can miss what matters for optimization. Under global depolarization, the mean normalized gap and the floor-corrected probability of every set of bitstrings, the optimum included, retain the same fraction of their noiseless improvement over uniform sampling. We test this prediction with depth-2, transferred-angle QAOA circuits for binary subproblems of an alternating-direction decomposition on the IBM Heron processor \texttt{ibm\_marrakesh}, with and without dynamical decoupling and twirling. At 12 qubits, the main-family circuits retained 29\% to 46\% of their mean-gap improvement but only 5\% to 15\% of their probability of the optimum, lower on at least nine of ten instances per run. Near-optimal bitstrings were lost about as much as the optimum, whereas the avoidance of poor bitstrings was retained best. In the first submission, a device-matched noise model reproduced the pattern but overestimated the retention of the optimum five- to eightfold. On a rugged planted family, the device found the optimum in 62\% of 768-shot blocks (noiseless: 98\%), within the range of local heuristics. Validations of optimization circuits should report retention of the optimum and of near-optimal sets.

papers.title: Intensity limits for phase-only holographic optical-tweezer arrays
papers.abstract: Optical tweezers use tightly focused laser beams to trap and manipulate individual particles, enabling advances in quantum computing, drug discovery, and biological research. Scaling these technologies to large arrays requires delivering sufficient light to every trapping site while minimizing the total laser power required. Here, we investigate the fundamental limits of how efficiently a phase-only hologram can distribute light across an array of optical traps. We derive upper bounds on the minimum intensity across trapping sites, accounting for illumination, target geometry, and diffraction from spatial light modulator pixels. For arrays arranged in a single plane or across two axial planes, we show how these limits scale with the number of traps and SLM pixels, and establish conditions for focusing light in three dimensions. Numerical experiments demonstrate that optimized holograms can closely approach these theoretical limits, suggesting that further improvements in phase optimization alone offer limited power savings. Instead, our results reveal how the choice of illumination and trap geometry can improve light efficiency, providing practical guidelines for designing larger, more power-efficient optical-tweezer arrays.

papers.title: Continual Instruction Tuning for LLM-ased Management of Continuum Resources
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for resource management across the Cloud-Edge continuum. However, embedding LLMs directly inside latency-sensitive control loops places inference latency, execution jitter, and hallucination risks on the critical path. This study argues for a different use of LLMs: a continually instruction-tuned intent compiler that runs once per management intent or declared context change, above a fast, deterministic tactical controller that handles all low-latency runtime actions. We formulate intent compilation as a continual instruction tuning problem, because management intents arrive sequentially and accumulate while infrastructure and workload contexts drift. Unlike recent LLM-based management frameworks, our design scores the model's outputs by execution, so that catastrophic forgetting can be measured in the executed objective of the underlying controller. On a continuum simulator with a 2B backbone and parameter-efficient adapters, preliminary results show that naive sequential tuning forgets earlier intents in the executed objective, that replay of stored examples nearly prevents this forgetting, and that the tuned compact compiler performs on par with simpler translators while being more robust than a grammar parser to rephrased intents.

papers.title: FAIDER: Fairness-Aware Item-Level Decoding for Large Language Model Recommenders
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) recommenders can produce semantically different recommendations when a user's protected attribute changes, even if the interaction history remains fixed. Controlling this disparity is challenging when model weights and full-vocabulary logits are inaccessible. We propose FAIDER (Fairness-Aware Item-level DEcoding for Recommendation), which incorporates fairness into list construction by selecting complete item candidates rather than manipulating token-level logits or repeatedly repairing finished outputs. The central idea is to separate the operational criterion for a violation from how strongly generation is constrained. Conformal-inspired empirical calibration fixes a cross-group semantic-disparity threshold, while online decoding applies either hard filtering or a soft penalty adjusted through dual-inspired feedback to target a prescribed violation rate. Separately, we establish a pathwise guarantee: under a uniform enforceability assumption, the soft decoder's empirical violation rate exceeds its target by at most $O(1/T)$. Experiments across recommendation benchmarks and LLM backbones show that Soft FAIDER improves both measured semantic fairness and ranking quality over the evaluated prompt-repair baselines. It also generally achieves a more favorable fairness-utility balance than the hard variant, indicating that stricter per-recommendation constraints do not necessarily yield lower measured disparity.

papers.title: TORNADO: Adaptive Latent Stochastic Transport for Calibrated Probabilistic PDE Forecasting
papers.abstract: Probabilistic neural surrogates for PDEs enable ensemble forecasting, but often exhibit miscalibration when used for uncertainty quantification, especially in compute-constrained, few-step inference regimes. Existing generative approaches typically rely on fixed global stochasticity, which cannot adapt predictive uncertainty to the local dynamical state. We propose TORNADO, a latent probabilistic forecasting framework that formulates next-step prediction as stochastic transport between VAE encoder posteriors. Unlike existing approaches with globally prescribed stochasticity, TORNADO learns a SDE with state-dependent diffusion, enabling the predictive uncertainty to adapt to the local latent dynamics. The model is trained using analytic conditional endpoint targets derived from a Gaussian interpolant, enabling simulation-free learning. An additional energy distance regularization term improves distributional alignment. Empirically, TORNADO improves uncertainty calibration over representative generative baselines, including stochastic interpolants, diffusion models, and flow matching, while maintaining comparable predictive accuracy. Our results show that adapting stochasticity to the latent state, rather than prescribing it globally, is an effective mechanism for improving calibration in practical neural PDE forecasting settings. Project page: https://tornado-sde.github.io.

papers.title: Key Institutional Considerations for Designing Effective Independent Verification Organizations
papers.abstract: Independent verification organizations (IVOs) have emerged as a popular, bipartisan solution for facilitating high-quality independent evaluations of AI technologies. But momentum is outpacing design: there is emerging consensus on the necessary operating conditions for robust IVOs, but little discourse on institutional and policy specifications to ensure those conditions are met. IVOs are currently envisioned primarily as a mechanism operating at the AI frontier and model level to evaluate catastrophic risks. Little work has yet been done on how to establish or enforce an IVO ecosystem that is equipped to handle myriad risks (i.e., beyond catastrophic ones) and operate at the system and application level across the deployment and use stages of the AI lifecycle. This paper argues that IVO design should ensure the capacity for evaluating AI models, systems, and applications in context for both frontier companies and enterprise companies & AI-adopting organizations. Additionally, this paper provides early considerations to advance IVO discourse from normative to operative, and from existential to everyday risks. Drawing from existing institutional constructs in financial services, education, public health, and science, we outline key considerations on whom IVOs serve, what access they require, how they interact with external governing structures, how they are funded, and how they fit into the wider assurance ecosystem. Much of the structure and knowledge necessary to holistically design IVOs and their ecosystem does not yet exist, even as companies rush to ink agreements with their chosen evaluators.

papers.title: Polarization Aware Deep Learning Framework for SAR Despeckling
papers.abstract: Speckle is an inherent characteristic of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery that complicates image interpretation and the extraction of reliable information. Although deep-learning-based despeckling methods have demonstrated promising performance, their applicability across different polarimetric configurations is often limited by the need for specialized architectures or separate training procedures. This paper presents a unified deep-learning framework for despeckling single-, dual-, and full-polarization SAR data using a single trained convolutional neural network. The proposed approach adopts a common nine-channel representation of the polarimetric covariance matrix and a polarization-aware masking strategy to accommodate different configurations without modifying the network architecture. Qualitative and quantitative comparison on three different scenes from different sensors demonstrate competitive performance across the considered experiments and support the feasibility of a unified, polarization-flexible approach to SAR despeckling across different polarimetric configurations.

papers.title: Raman anyon-Hubbard model in a 1D Bose lattice gas
papers.abstract: The anyon-Hubbard model is the paradigmatic lattice model of one-dimensional (1D) anyons, in which chiral interactions make bosons equivalent to particles with fractional statistics. Its continuum limit, the chiral BF theory, emerges as the low-energy description of a Raman-coupled Bose gas with imbalanced interactions. Here, we show that loading such a gas into a 1D optical lattice realizes the lattice counterpart of this theory, which we name the Raman anyon-Hubbard model. The Raman-dressed bosons acquire density-dependent Peierls phases when tunneling through occupied sites. For a small statistical phase, the model reduces to the anyon-Hubbard model, while beyond this limit it defines a distinct lattice anyon model with unbounded rather than periodic statistical interactions. Numerically, we show that the dressed gas displays the defining properties of 1D anyons, namely a density-dependent asymmetry of the ground-state momentum distribution, interaction-induced asymmetric transport and chiral bound states. Remarkably, these features are readily accessible with Raman-coupled $^{39}$K atoms, opening up the experimental exploration of 1D anyons beyond the few-particle regime.

papers.title: Knowing When to Intervene: Causal Evaluation of AI Agents
papers.abstract: Current evaluations of agentic AI systems primarily rely on benchmarks. However, the static nature of benchmarks makes them uninformative about the value of auditing interventions at deployment time. For reliable deployment, we often need to determine within an agent's trajectory whether or not to intervene, e.g., by verifying the agent's current output or steering it toward different behavior, using either human review or more costly models or time-consuming agentic supervision. The value of such interventions is fundamentally a causal inference question, asking whether the causal effect of such an intervention is beneficial for the final outcome. Estimating this causal effect is particularly challenging due to the dynamic nature of the problem: the impact of an intervention depends on the current context and environment, as well as the agent's future behavior. We develop the first methodologically grounded framework for evaluating the causal effects of randomized interventions within agent trajectories. By leveraging a relatively small dataset of agent trajectories collected under randomized interventions such as verification or screening, we can estimate the dynamic causal effect of a rich class of (contextual) intervention policies. The structural parameters that we estimate can also be used to construct safety leaderboards that capture the risk of various agentic actions, which can be used by practitioners for audit prioritization. Applying our methods to tau-bench Retail, ToolSandbox, and ImpossibleBench, we find that intervention effects vary substantially across agent actions and states. More broadly, our work suggests a rich research agenda at the intersection of causal inference and agentic evaluation, which we believe is essential for the reliable and safe deployment of AI agents in the real world.

papers.title: ODEAction: From Predicting Chunks to Evolving Actions
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models typically generate actions in chunks, dividing continuous robot execution into separately predicted action chunks, which can introduce discontinuities at chunk boundaries. We propose ODEAction, a chunk-free action generation paradigm that replaces action chunk prediction with Continuous Action Evolution. We use an ordinary differential equation (ODE) to describe the continuous evolution of actions, and define the vector field of this ODE as the Action Transition Field to characterize how actions evolve with respect to evolution time. During inference, the model takes the current action as the initial condition and numerically solves the ODE defined by the learned Action Transition Field, thereby recursively generating subsequent actions with explicit dependencies. ODEAction is implemented as a modular action head that can be integrated with different vision-language backbones. Experiments on LIBERO, EBench, RoboTwin, and real-robot tasks show that, compared with action-chunk-based baselines, ODEAction improves both task performance and trajectory quality, with particularly pronounced gains on fine manipulation tasks.

papers.title: DKWBC: Decoupling Motion Tracking and Balancing for Humanoid Whole-Body Control
papers.abstract: Humanoid whole-body control requires a robot to track diverse reference motions while maintaining balance under gravity, torque limits, contact switching, and external disturbances. Existing reinforcement-learning-based trackers typically learn control outputs that jointly address motion tracking and balance. However, similar reference poses can correspond to substantially different dynamic demands, requiring a unified policy to learn motion-dependent control requirements alongside balance corrections. This can complicate learning and lead to high-frequency fluctuations in control outputs. We propose DKWBC, a dynamics-informed whole-body control framework that combines explicit model-based tracking with a learned balancing residual. Inspired by the model-based and environmental-wrench contributions to joint torques in floating-base dynamics, DKWBC uses inverse-dynamics feedforward and joint PD feedback to supply tracking torques, while a residual policy learns additional joint-torque corrections for balanced execution. By explicitly accounting for motion-dependent torque demands, this structure simplifies the policy's learning task. Experiments in simulation and on real hardware demonstrate that a single learned balancing policy generalizes across motion datasets while maintaining accurate motion tracking and balance across ground support, attached payloads, and physical interaction. Project page: https://robbyant-research.github.io/DKWBC/.

papers.title: Fujita's Very Ampleness Conjecture for $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$-Bundles over Curves
papers.abstract: Let $\mathcal{E}$ be a vector bundle of rank $n\geq 2$ over a smooth projective curve $C$ over $\mathbb{C}$. We prove that $ω_{\mathbb{P}_C(\mathcal{E})}\otimes\mathcal{L}_1\otimes\dots\otimes\mathcal{L}_k$ is very ample for arbitrary ample line bundles $\mathcal{L}_i$ on ${\mathbb{P}_C(\mathcal{E})}$ when $k\geq n+2$.

papers.title: On derandomizing the line-point low-degree test
papers.abstract: We investigate the derandomized version of the classical line-point low-degree test in the high-error regime in the bivariate setting and reveal some unexpected behavior. The classical line-point low-degree test takes an $m$-variate function $f$ over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$, queries it along a random line and accepts if the restriction of the function to this line is a low-degree polynomial. The high-error version of (the analysis of) this test asserts that if $f$ has at least $ε$ expected local agreement with a degree-$k$ univariate polynomial on a random line, then in fact $f$ is non-trivially close to some degree-$k$ $m$-variate polynomial even as $ε$ approaches $0$ (provided $q$ is sufficiently large compared to $k$ and $1/ε$). The derandomized version of the problem asks if the same holds when the line is not chosen uniformly over all possible lines but rather from a small set. In this paper we explore the bivariate case ($m=2$). We show, somewhat surprisingly, that there exists a function $f\colon \mathbb{F}_q^2 \to \mathbb{F}_q$ and a set of lines $\mathcal{L}$ in $\mathbb{F}_q^2$ of size nearly $q^{3/2}$ such that on every line in $\mathcal{L}$, $f$ has agreement $\approx 1/2$ on average with some univariate polynomial of degree $k=\sqrt{q}/2$ and yet $f$ is $1 - O(q^{-1/2})$ far from every polynomial of degree $O(k)$. On the positive side, we show that once the field size $q$ is at least $k^2/(ε)^{O(1)}$ such examples disappear and we can get sets of lines of size $O(q/ε^{O(1)})$ on which the low-degree test has a high-error analysis. On the way to our positive result, we show a new high-degree version of the classical two-direction Polishchuk--Spielman divisibility lemma.

papers.title: On the optimal mass threshold for the two-dimensional Keller-Segel system coupled to the Navier-Stokes equations
papers.abstract: We investigate the mass threshold for the two-dimensional Keller-Segel system coupled with the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. In the absence of fluid interaction, the classical Keller-Segel system admits a well-known $4π$-critical-mass dichotomy: for every suitably regular initial datum of total mass $m<4π$, the associated no-flux initial-boundary value problem admits a global bounded classical solution, whereas for $m>4π$, there exist smooth initial configurations of mass $m$ such that the associated solution blows up in finite or infinite time. For the fluid-coupled system, Winkler ({SIAM J. Math. Anal.}, 52:2041-2080, 2020) first established global generalized solvability under the condition $m<2π$ and posed an open question whether the fluid action may lower the critical blow-up mass to some value lying between $2π$ and $4π$. Based on numerical evidence, Bonilla and Gutiérrez-Santacreu ({J. Numer. Math.}, 32:175-212, 2024) later conjectured that the critical value is still $4π$. In the present work, we resolve this open problem and provide a rigorous mathematical proof to the conjecture, which indicates that the presence of the fluid does not alter the critical mass threshold, and the entire classical subcritical regime remains intact---every admissible initial datum with total mass $m<4π$ generates a unique global classical solution that is uniformly bounded in time. Our proof relies on the construction of a new quasi-energy inequality. The key underlying observation is that combining relative isoperimetric estimates with rearrangement techniques yields a Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality on bounded planar domains with an explicit leading constant.

papers.title: PathXAI: Evidence-guided structured pathology reporting by transferable tissue segmentation
papers.abstract: Pathology reporting translates tissue observations across regions and slides into diagnoses and supporting morphological descriptions, yet explicit tissue-composition measurements are rarely used to guide H&E-based report generation. We developed PathXAI, which pairs transferable tissue segmentation with a pretrained vision-language model. Because supplying tissue information directly with H&E images gave limited benefit, PathXAI-Report uses segmentation overlays and tissue statistics in separate steps, selects between candidate diagnoses by fixed rules, acquires further images when evidence is insufficient and records every step for review, without updating model weights. Its segmentation component exceeded baselines in mean Dice on internal and external tests. In automated evaluation on 1,200 public and 151 private cases, PathXAI achieved higher agreement with reference diagnoses and documented morphology than H&E-based comparators. On the public cohort, it exceeded Qwen+H&E by 4.4 percentage points in cancer family match rate and 5.7 percentage points in finding F1.

papers.title: Slim Polygons, Hyperbolicity, and a new Quasi-Isometric Invariant
papers.abstract: We introduce the slimness function, $\mathrm{Slim}_X(n)$, of a geodesic metric space, which records the maximal slimness of its geodesic polygons as a function of the number of sides. We study the large-scale behaviour of this function and its relation to hyperbolicity, growth function, and quasi-isometries. We first establish that the slimness function is a natural quasi-isometric invariant in the hyperbolic setting. We then obtain quantitative estimates for geodesic polygons in hyperbolic spaces and bounded-valency graphs. In particular, we show that sufficiently slow growth of the slimness function forces tree-like geometry. We also prove a decomposition result for trees of hyperbolic spaces. We show that for a finitely generated hyperbolic group $G$ there are only two possibilities: either $G$ is virtually free and $\operatorname{Slim}_G$ is bounded, or $\operatorname{Slim}_G(n)\simeq\log n$. Finally, we investigate the interaction between polygonal slimness and the growth of connected bounded-valency graphs. Combining the resulting estimates with large-scale dimension theory, we obtain criteria implying that an unbounded graph has asymptotic dimension one.

papers.title: Stabilizing Vector Approximate Message Passing with Circuit-Designed Lag-Lead Damping
papers.abstract: Vector approximate message passing (VAMP) often fails to converge on ill-conditioned matrices, and its damping factor is tuned either manually or adaptively. Using the fact that VAMP iterations are the discretization of an electric circuit, we show that the denoiser and the likelihood act as nonlinear resistors, the Onsager correction is a mirror resistor and damping is a lag filter. This circuit gives a closed-form loop gain whose spectrum can predict when VAMP fails. Because a lag filter cannot isolate the oscillating modes, we add a lead capacitor whose design often results in a negative capacitance. Across a wide range of condition numbers, our proposed damping strategy achieves a higher convergence rate than adaptive damping and Anderson acceleration at a lower mean iteration cost. On ill-conditioned multipath channels, across ranks and sparsity levels, it also converges more reliably than existing damping baselines.

papers.title: Generalized Hopf bifurcations: a homological analysis and obstructions to their existence
papers.abstract: A generalized Hopf bifurcation takes place when varying a parameter of a (semi)dynamical system causes an attractor $K$ to become a repeller. In doing so, it expels a (parameter-dependent) family of attractors. In this paper we concentrate on two questions: (1) what do the expelled attractors look like?, and (2) can any attractor $K$ undergo a generalized Hopf bifurcation? Regarding (1), we compute the cohomology of the expelled attractors in terms of the cohomology of $K$; in the case of continuous-time dynamics this can be improved to a computation of their Borsuk shape. As for (2), we show that certain compacta cannot undergo generalized Hopf bifurcations and, when the ambient space has dimension $ \leq 3$, give a complete topological characterization of which can.

papers.title: Adjustment-Anchor Dependence in Formulaic Alpha Languages: A Certified Grammar and a Re-Anchoring Audit
papers.abstract: Several public scripts for formulaic alpha mining store prices adjusted to the snapshot's last day, so a past day's stored price changes with every later split or dividend and formulas that do not cancel the adjustment factor depend on future corporate actions. We formalise a change of adjustment anchor as a per-stock group action and give a two-sorted type system that soundly certifies anchor invariance from a formula's syntax, under a declared field-adjustment contract and idealised operator semantics; its second sort admits log-returns, and a linear-time checker plugs into any miner. In a re-anchoring audit on Chinese A-shares, pools that five published methods mined in our benchmark pipeline score a mean information coefficient (IC) 0.005 higher on the stored representation than on a cutoff-anchored one, about 14% of their IC. The mean signed change for certified pools is about -0.001, and pools mined on past-anchored data stay sensitive. On the Chinese development folds, certification shows no detectable predictive cost or gain; the estimated minimum detectable difference is about 0.017 IC across cells on pool ICs of 0.03-0.04. We also trace an erroneous index-membership entry to public Qlib data snapshots and show that re-mining exposes the effect of such data defects, which re-evaluating fixed pools understates.

papers.title: Weyl Rescalings: A First Order Approach
papers.abstract: Weyl transformations, --local rescalings in which the metric transforms as $g_{μν}(x)\longrightarrow Ω^2(x)\, g_{μν}(x)$--, are expected to be a symmetry of nature at extremely high energy, that should be (spontaneously) broken at low energy. In Cartan's first order formulation of gravity this translates into the condition that the local frames (vielbein) scale as $e^a(x) \longrightarrow Ω(x) e^a(x)$. In this construction, the Lorentz connection one-form fields $ω^a{}_b$ are independent from $e^a$, and since Lorentz transformations and dilatations commute, $ω$ and $R(ω)$ must be Weyl invariant, while in the second order metric formalism the Ricci tensor undergoes a non-homogeneous transformation. This generates a tension between the two formulations, which should be equivalent in the vanishing torsion limit. Here we show how the puzzle can be resolved taking into account the role of torsion. This also sheds some light on the conformal coupling of matter fields to gravity.

papers.title: The strong fractional choice number can exceed the choice number by an arbitrarily large amount
papers.abstract: Erdős, Rubin and Taylor asked whether $(a,b)$-choosability implies $(am,bm)$-choosability for all positive integers $a,b,m$. Dvořák, Hu and Sereni disproved this for $(a,b,m)=(4,1,2)$ and asked whether a $3$-choosable graph can fail to be $(6,2)$-choosable. Following an earlier discussion by Jiang and Zhu, Li and Zhu asked whether every $k$-choosable graph is $(kb+1,b)$-choosable. Equivalently, Xu and Zhu asked whether $\mathrm{ch}_f^s(G)\le\mathrm{ch}(G)$ for every graph $G$, where $\mathrm{ch}(G)$ is its choice number and $\mathrm{ch}_f^s(G)$ is its strong fractional choice number, defined as the infimum of the real numbers $r$ such that $G$ is $(a,b)$-choosable for all positive integers $a,b$ with $a/b\ge r$. In this paper, we prove that, for all integers $t\ge0$ and $b\ge7t+2$, there is a planar graph of choice number three that is not $(3b+t,b)$-choosable. This answers the question of Dvořák, Hu and Sereni affirmatively and the other questions negatively, even for planar graphs. Next, for all integers $k\ge4$, $t\ge0$ and $b\ge3t+2$, we construct a graph of choice number $k$ that is not $(kb+t,b)$-choosable, using only the six-vertex wheel $W_5$ as its core gadget. The case $t=0$ and $b=2$ recovers the result of Dvořák, Hu and Sereni. The supremum of $\mathrm{ch}_f^s(G)-\mathrm{ch}(G)$ is at least $1/7$ over planar graphs of choice number three, and at least $1/3$ over graphs of choice number $k$ for each $k\ge4$. Finally, for every sufficiently large integer $k$, we construct a graph $G$ with $\mathrm{ch}(G)=k$ that is not $(2k+t,2)$-choosable, where $t\ge C\sqrt{k}$ for an absolute constant $C>0$. Thus the gap is unbounded even with multiplicity fixed at two. We further obtain $k+Ω(\sqrt{k})\le\sup\{\mathrm{ch}_f^s(G):\mathrm{ch}(G)=k\}\le2^{(1+o(1))k}$ as $k$ tends to infinity.

papers.title: Before the First Bond: Depletion-Assisted Stochastic Capture at the Onset of Endocytosis
papers.abstract: The first barrier to receptor-mediated endocytosis is not binding but arrival within a few nanometers of the membrane. In a crowded extracellular environment, this pre-contact approach is driven by thermal fluctuations and entropic depletion, yet continuum models usually start from established contact or treat the approach deterministically. We formulate a thermodynamically consistent stochastic theory for this stage. The sphere--plane depletion geometry uses the exact Asakura--Oosawa spherical-cap overlap, not a fitted cap, with either ideal van~'t~Hoff or pressure-only Carnahan--Starling (CS) pressure. Near-wall mobility enters with its essential and often omitted noise-induced drift. The first specific reaction is a Robin radiation boundary; the outer boundary is reflecting or absorbing. Three first-passage quantities are obtained analytically by quadrature: the mean reaction time, the reaction-before-escape probability, and the conditional success time, the last encoded by a Doob transform that exposes the selection bias of conditioning on capture. The local Damköhler number diagnoses the boundary reaction-to-diffusion ratio, while the mean-time crossover follows from the exact reaction and diffusion terms. At baseline, ideal and CS contact depths are \(2.33\) and \(5.95\,k_{\rm B}T\), and the reflecting-outer mean reaction time is approximately \(0.20\,{\rm ms}\); with an absorbing outer boundary the conditional success time is shorter, but the two observables use different boundary protocols. Numerical checks reproduce the analytic results and the radiation-boundary mass balance. This provides a quantitative theoretical framework for crowding-assisted capture before membrane wrapping.

papers.title: Distributed Inner-Product Estimation for Continuous-Variable Quantum States
papers.abstract: Distributed inner-product estimation (DIPE) is a fundamental task in quantum information, aiming to estimate the inner product between two unknown quantum states prepared on separate quantum platforms. In multimode continuous-variable (CV) systems, the infinite-dimensional Hilbert space poses additional challenges. In this work, we propose a protocol for CV-DIPE that requires the two platforms to share a common phase reference and perform local homodyne measurements at the same randomly sampled phase settings, followed by classical post-processing of the measurement data. We derive explicit upper bounds on the sample complexity of this protocol. These bounds depend on the available physical prior information. Specifically, we provide bounds for two natural cases: finite-energy states and Gaussian states. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate the theoretical performance of this estimation scheme. Our findings offer a CV-DIPE protocol that relies solely on homodyne measurements and remains applicable even when neither of the two quantum states is fully characterized.

papers.title: Block-exchange descent for insertion: commuting projections and minimum masks
papers.abstract: For fixed nonempty words $u,v$, the minimum insertion degree of a shuffle is the least number of inserted-source runs among its representations. We prove that, after a block exchange from a minimum mask of degree $r$, the minimum over masks with commuting source projections is exactly $r-1$; a larger decrease occurs precisely when a noncommuting mask has fewer runs. If either source is unary, every such exchange is exact. We prove an explicit repair for an infinite periodic degree-three family. Computer-assisted results establish first-mask descent through combined length seventeen over every alphabet, degree-three first-mask descent through length thirty, and a uniform repair of all degree-three failures through length thirty, including all further letter identifications. Counterexamples to arbitrary, first, and last minimum-mask choices explain the need for alternative masks. Finally, we prove that minimum iteration depths have no gaps for arbitrary languages. General block-exchange descent and Singleton No-Gap remain open.

papers.title: Planarity estimates and classification of ancient flows at the Andrews-Baker threshold
papers.abstract: We study space-time proper ancient solutions of the mean curvature flow of $n$-dimensional submanifolds of $\mathbb R^{n+p}$ that are uniformly quadratically pinched up to the Andrews-Baker threshold $\frac{4}{3n}$. We prove codimension reduction and convexity: every such solution is either a static affine $n$-plane, or a flow of hypersurfaces of a fixed affine $(n+1)$-dimensional subspace whose time slices bound convex bodies. By results of Bourni, Langford and Lynch and of Bamler and Lai, the flow is then noncollapsed, and it is a family of shrinking spheres or cylinders, an ancient oval, a bowl soliton or a flying wing, possibly times a Euclidean factor. Space-time properness replaces the finite entropy and polynomial curvature growth assumptions of Lee, Naff and Zhu. The main tool is a parabolically scale-invariant interior planarity estimate for $n\geq5$, obtained from Naff's gradient estimates through a localization argument in the spirit of Ecker and Huisken. In dimensions five and six, where these estimates do not give the gradient terms a sign, we bound them from below as in a previous work. The same localization, applied to the gradient estimate of Lynch and Nguyen and to a second order analogue, gives the derivative bounds from which convexity follows. For closed flows, we extend Lynch's planarity estimate to a larger range of exponents.

papers.title: Learning to Reason from Reference Samples Alone: Reinforced Adversarial Learning for Modern LLM Post-Training
papers.abstract: In many settings where LLM post-training is desirable, high-quality answers are recognizable but difficult to score with explicit rewards. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is limited to tasks where an explicit correctness signal is available. Prior adversarial approaches to training reasoning LLMs either complement verifiable rewards with co-trained critics or require reference reasoning traces. We ask whether a co-trained LLM judge can turn reference answers alone into the sole reward for on-policy post-training of reasoning LLMs. We call this method Reinforced Adversarial Learning (RAL). We first validate RAL on three verifiable tasks (integer multiplication, code-based arithmetic-expression synthesis, and SMILES-to-formula translation), using the verifiers only for evaluation. With sufficiently capable judges and enough training, RAL matches direct RLVR. We then apply RAL to scientific abstract generation in two settings. In the first setting, RAL guides the generator to produce abstracts in the scientific domain of the reference abstracts, even though the prompt leaves that domain unspecified. In the second setting, we generate abstracts for U.S. National Institutes of Health grant proposals conditioned on the grant title. Human scientists and an ensemble of LLM judges find our generations harder to distinguish from real abstracts than those of frontier-LLM baselines. These results suggest a path toward post-training reasoning models in scientific and other high-value domains, where increasingly capable judges infer hard-to-specify reward functions from example answers.

papers.title: Vietoris-Rips complexes of affine Coxeter groups
papers.abstract: We prove that all affine Coxeter groups admit contractible Vietoris-Rips complexes. More precisely, for any affine Coxeter group $W_a$ with standard generating set $S$, we prove that the Vietoris-Rips complex $\mathcal{VR}_t(W_a;S)$ is contractible for all sufficiently large $t$. We also investigate other finitely generated groups of the form $G=H\rtimes F$ for $F$ finite, and prove that for any finite symmetric generating set $A$ for $H$ such that $A^F=A$, the complexes $\mathcal{VR}_t(G;AF)$ and $\mathcal{VR}_t(H;A)$ are homotopy equivalent for all $t\ge 1$.

papers.title: Negative-Power Density of States in Chiral-Orthogonal Disordered Systems and the IR Phase of QCD
papers.abstract: The recently discovered IR phase of QCD is characterized by an infrared (IR) sector of Dirac modes that separates and dynamically decouples from the bulk of the spectrum, becoming scale invariant in the process [1]. Among key features of this IR sector is the negative power-law behavior of Dirac spectral density near zero with power close to $-1$. Here we start investigating to what extent can this behavior be mimicked by chiral Anderson models. In particular, we study 3-D chiral-orthogonal systems with logarithmic off-diagonal disorder where negative-power ``spikes'' have been observed [2]. We find that for disorders of moderate strength $W$, these models in fact do not have a power-singular density of states (DOS) at zero energy in the thermodynamic limit. Rather, the corresponding power vanishes but the spectrum features a very accurate negative-power behavior on an interval around $E=1$, spreading increasingly closer to $E=0$ and $E=\infty$ with increasing $W$. We connect this to the fact that random hoppings $t$ in these quantum systems are drawn from a scale-invariant $1/t$ distribution regularized via $t \in [e^{-W/2}, e^{W/2}]$, and DOS with negative power can naturally arise inside that range. In fact, we find that power $p$ in the vicinity of energy $E$ satisfies $\lim_{W \to \infty} p(W, E) = -1$ for all $E$ we access. This indicates that, upon removing the cutoff $W$, quantum mechanics transforms the scale-invariant $1/t$ noise into a scale-invariant $1/E$ distribution of eigenstates, which mimics the interpretation of scale-invariant Dirac spectral densities in the IR phase as being due to scale-invariant glue backgrounds [1]. Our results imply that, when modeling the IR phase, the IR cutoff in chiral Anderson systems needs to be tied to their randomness strength $W$ rather than to their lattice size $L$.

papers.title: Can One Hear Geometry? Gauge-Invariant Spectral Descriptors for Text-to-B-rep Retrieval
papers.abstract: Text-to-3D solid retrieval faces a fundamental representation gap: while natural language describes intrinsic shapes, Boundary Representation (B-rep) entangles precise geometry with arbitrary variations in pose, scale, and boundary encoding conventions. Existing methods either discretize B-reps at the cost of analytic precision, or learn features from topological graphs without explicit invariance guarantees. We propose **SpectraBRep** (*Spectral Geometry for Text-to-B-rep Retrieval*), a framework based on geometric invariance and spectral descriptors that mathematically eliminates representation ambiguities prior to cross-modal alignment. Formalizing translation, rotation, reflection, uniform scaling, and contour re-indexing via group actions, we exploit the planar-profile-and-extrusion structure of engineering solids to construct a unified spectral descriptor across cross-sectional regions, contour boundaries, and extrusion depths. On public benchmarks, our method achieves state-of-the-art recall performance across all evaluation metrics.

papers.title: Timelike Supersymmetric Geometries in Seven-Dimensional Supergravity
papers.abstract: Seven-dimensional supergravity poses a uniquely intricate supersymmetry problem, combining topologically massive higher-form gauge dynamics, distinct Clifford algebra properties, and rich geometric structures. We first establish the complete formulation of the maximal Cartan-gauged theory in terms of the gauge-invariant higher-form flux, including both the bosonic action and supersymmetry variations. This formulation, which also makes the smooth ungauged limit manifest, is achieved by requiring a consistent truncation to the minimal Cartan-gauged theory in the equal-charge limit. We construct the complete bilinear system for a timelike Killing vector, where additional internal orientation of the symplectic-Majorana spinor arises already in the scalar sector, uniquely among pure minimal ungauged theories. In the equal-charge sector, we decouple the algebraic constraints into SU$(3)$-isotypic components, and analyse the differential bilinear relations, determining the permitted dilaton gradient, fluxes, fibration twist and intrinsic torsion of the base. We prove that with gauging and active Cartan flux, the complex scalar bilinear vanishes identically. We also construct a Killing gauge for the higher-form potential compatible with the self-duality condition. We show that with gauging but no active Cartan flux, the Killing vector also acts as a generator of the gauged R-symmetry, and the base structure is enlarged from SU$(3)$ to U$(3)$. We find that BPS-flow solutions realize this setting. With supersymmetry, we isolate a single independent component of the 3-form equation across an exhaustive four-class partition for both theories within this setup. Applied to known and proposed solutions in both theories, this classification exposes unexplored sectors and provides an accessible toolbox for constructing and testing solutions and developing new geometric and holographic applications.

papers.title: Sharp Quantitative Convergence of Compactly Supported Aggregation-Diffusion
papers.abstract: We establish the quantitative convergence of nonlinear aggregation-diffusion equations in dimension one, with sublinear attraction kernel and degenerate diffusion higher than quadratic. In these models, steady state is known to be the unique, compactly supported, and radial decreasing probability distribution. In this paper, we work with compactly supported densities in dimension one, we prove these solutions converge to the steady state exponentially fast.

papers.title: Is the Kaniadakis deformation of holographic dark energy detectable? A non-flat analysis with DESI DR2, cosmic chronometers and Pantheon+SH0ES
papers.abstract: Kaniadakis entropy deforms the horizon entropy through one parameter $κ$, and holographic dark energy built on it (KHDE) reduces to standard holographic dark energy (HDE) when $κ\to0$. The deformation enters the equations through the dimensionless combination $β=KM_p^2/H_0^2$, where $K$ is the effective KHDE parameter. We test whether current data detect it in a curved universe without CMB information. We combine Pantheon+SH0ES supernovae calibrated with Cepheids, 32 cosmic-chronometer measurements of $H(z)$ with their correlated systematic errors, and DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillations with a free sound horizon. Non-flat KHDE fits the data as well as flat $Λ$CDM ($Δχ^2=-3.0$), but $β$ is not detected: the profile $χ^2$ changes by only 0.44 between $β=0$ and its best value, and by 0.46 in the flat case. The upper limit $β<0.65$ (95%) comes from the condition that the model has a real solution, not from the data; where the truncated expansion is reliable, the limit is $β<0.57$. $β$ of order one corresponds to $κ$ of order $10^{-122}$. Comparing flat and non-flat HDE and KHDE with $Λ$CDM shows that neither curvature nor the deformation improves the fit enough to justify the extra parameters. The joint fit gives $Ω_{k0}=0.007\pm0.046$, $H_0=72.85\pm0.94$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ and $r_d=137.41\pm1.88$ Mpc. The expansion starts to accelerate at $z_t=0.66\pm0.03$, and a neural-network reconstruction of $H(z)$ from the chronometers agrees with the model.

papers.title: Generalizable fetal brain biometry via adaptive artificial intelligence
papers.abstract: Fetal brain biometry provides a quantitative basis for assessing prenatal growth and identifying congenital brain abnormalities. However, comprehensive assessment remains limited by labor-intensive manual measurements and automated models that lose accuracy across imaging sequences and institutions. We introduce BioTTA, an anatomically guided test-time adaptation framework that measures 11 fetal brain biometrics from reconstructed three-dimensional magnetic resonance images. BioTTA adapts pretrained models to individual unlabeled volumes using geometric consistency and atlas priors, without access to source images. In a retrospective study across five centers in China and Switzerland, BioTTA improved measurement accuracy across three out-of-distribution datasets and two network architectures. It reduced mean absolute measurement errors by 46-82% relative to the corresponding models without adaptation, achieving errors similar to those of supervised fine-tuning. Its measurements were mapped onto normative growth trajectories derived from expert annotations, enabling gestational-age-specific assessment through a web-based reporting platform. Across four disease cohorts, the platform achieved 82.1-95.0% accuracy in binary detection of ventriculomegaly or cerebellar abnormalities, with performance similar to that of a senior radiologist. BioTTA provides a practical foundation for standardized fetal brain biometry across heterogeneous imaging settings, supporting scalable prenatal growth assessment and quantitative evaluation of brain abnormalities.

papers.title: Khovanov and knot Floer homology of fibered positive links
